---
title: "Binary Logic: Questions That Select"
---

A die shows four. Is it even? Yes. Is it greater than four? No.

These questions turn a numerical value into a truth value. Once we can do that, logic becomes a way to select observations.

## 🔰 A predicate makes a distinction {#sec-sample-binary-logic-a-predicate-makes-a-distinction}

Let

$$
A(f)=\mathbf1_{\{f\text{ is even}\}}.
$$

The indicator is one when the condition holds and zero otherwise. Its output belongs to the Boolean type $\{0,1\}$.

The zero means the condition is false for this input. It does not mean the input was absent, unreadable, or not yet observed. Missing knowledge needs a separate representation.

For the record $S=(1,2,2,5)$, evaluation gives

$$
A(S)=(0,1,1,0).
$$

We have constructed a binary signal from a numerical one.

## 🏵 Combine the questions {#sec-sample-binary-logic-combine-the-questions}

For truth values $a,b\in\{0,1\}$, the usual operations have simple arithmetic forms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\neg a&=1-a,\\
a\land b&=ab,\\
a\lor b&=a+b-ab,\\
a\mathbin{\mathrm{XOR}}b&=a+b-2ab.
\end{aligned}
$$

Check the four inputs:

- $(0,0)$ gives AND $0$, OR $0$, XOR $0$.
- $(0,1)$ gives AND $0$, OR $1$, XOR $1$.
- $(1,0)$ gives AND $0$, OR $1$, XOR $1$.
- $(1,1)$ gives AND $1$, OR $1$, XOR $0$.

OR includes the case where both conditions hold. XOR selects exactly one.

For the true-or-false inputs, these formulas stay inside the Boolean type. Extending them to other numbers requires a new contract.

## ⚙️ Logic on outcomes becomes algebra on events {#sec-sample-binary-logic-logic-on-outcomes-becomes-algebra-on-events}

Let $A$ be the event “even,” and $B$ the event “greater than three.” For a die,

$$
A=\{2,4,6\},\qquad B=\{4,5,6\}.
$$

Then:

- $A\cap B=\{4,6\}$: both conditions hold.
- $A\cup B=\{2,4,5,6\}$: at least one holds.
- $A^c=\{1,3,5\}$: the first condition fails.
- $A\mathbin{\triangle}B=\{2,5\}$: exactly one holds.

The complement is relative to the declared universe $\{1,\ldots,6\}$. We need that universe to know what lies outside $A$.

## 💡 Summing weights explains the addition rule {#sec-sample-binary-logic-summing-weights-explains-the-addition-rule}

When we add the probability of $A$ to that of $B$, their overlap is counted twice. Removing one copy gives

$$
\mathbb P(A\cup B)
=
\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B).
$$

For our fair die, this is

$$
\frac12+\frac12-\frac13=\frac23.
$$

The Boolean product $A(f)B(f)$ determines whether one outcome belongs to the intersection. Multiplying the probabilities $\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)$ is a different operation: it gives intersection probability only under independence. Here that product would be $1/4$, which is incorrect.

## ☯ A boundary can be exact while our knowledge is uncertain {#sec-sample-binary-logic-a-boundary-can-be-exact-while-our-knowledge-is-uncertain}

The face is even or it is not. Before looking, we may assign probability $1/2$ to evenness. That uncertainty does not make the face half-even.

[Fuzzy Logic](fuzzy-logic.qmd) asks a different question: what if the description itself allows partial membership?

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try the idea {#sec-sample-binary-logic-try-the-idea}

Let $A$ mean “even” and $B$ mean “six.” Is the inclusive OR different from $A$? Is XOR different? Are the events mutually exclusive?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Work it through {#sec-sample-binary-logic-work-it-through}

Since $B\subseteq A$, inclusive OR is just $A=\{2,4,6\}$. XOR removes six and gives $\{2,4\}$. The events are not mutually exclusive because six belongs to both. XOR is an operation we can apply to overlapping events; mutual exclusion is a property of the events themselves.
:::
